So and neither are two words that along with the appropriate auxiliary verb can help us show agreement or disagreement with what another person says or thinks.

When using the simple present tense, if you agree with what a person says you can use so + auxiliary verb + subject.

Examples:

A: I’m interested in acquiring a new management system for the company.

B: So am I.

A: I think this Software License Agreement is necessary.

B: So do I.

However, if you agree with a negative statement about what another says or does, you can use neither + auxiliary verb + subject.

A: I'm not quite sure of buying this software.

B: Neither am I.

A: That software license it's too expensive and limited, I don't like it.

B: Neither do I.
I don't think an inexpensive license offers what we need. Neither do I.
I think we cannot take any chances with this kind of things. So do I.

Before using any kind of software, the user needs to understand the kind of software licensing they have to accept. This kind of license not only protects the manufacturers and producers but it also informs the end user about how software can be used and what they can or cannot do.

Depending on the needs and the purchasing power of the end user, there are different kinds of software licensing that can be grouped into two big categories Public Domain Software and Commercial Software:

Public Domain Software

A software that has no owner of the intellectual property. It can be edited, changed, copied, and distributed with no restrictions.

Will: So, now that we have everything, we need to decide the kind of software we're going to be using.
Phil: Let's just download it from the internet. I know a few websites that can do the trick.
Will: What? Are you out of your mind? We need to sign a software license agreement. A kind of legal contract, you know.
Phil: Really? Why?

Will: Well, for starters, our business is all about design, right? And if we want to be deemed as a serious company, I think we need to purchase the proper and legal software. I don't think an inexpensive license offers what we need.
Phil: Neither do I.
Will: We need to procure a reliable software from a software vendor. For that, a software license agreement, where both the vendor's and our rights and obligations are specified. is mandatory. I think we cannot take any chances with this kind of things.
Phil: So do I. But aren't those licenses too restrictive?

Will: Well, they do give the customer limited permission to use the licensed software and they also impose some obligation on the customers. However, they also establish the software vendor's limited promises regarding the availability of certain services and the quality of the software. They also allocate the risk between the software vendor and the licensee.

Phil: In other words, we're more protected with a software license agreement.

Will: Exactly. And this kind of license can take various forms. The cheap commercial off-the-shelf software administered by a non-negotiable standard form agreement which is accepted by the customer before or during the software installation process; or the expensive software which comes with an agreement subject to negotiation by the software vendor and the customer.
